before: One submitted name can have several values. A multiple select preserves each selected option as a separate name/value pair; it does not automatically join those values into one comma-separated string.

multiple permits multiple selections. size="4" requests four visible rows, not a four-choice limit. optgroup label names a group of options; it is not itself a selectable answer. option value is the data value, while its text is the visible choice. selected sets an initial selection. Without required, selecting nothing is allowed.

```html
<form id="seeds">
  <label for="choices">Seeds to request</label>
  <select id="choices" name="seed" multiple size="4">
    <optgroup label="Herbs"><option value="basil" selected>Basil</option><option value="dill">Dill</option></optgroup>
    <optgroup label="Flowers"><option value="poppy" selected>Poppy</option></optgroup>
  </select>
  <button type="submit">Request seeds</button>
</form>
```
Initially this form contributes seed=basil and seed=poppy, in document order. The supplied checker uses FormData.getAll("seed") to inspect all local values; that is test infrastructure, not an HTML function to implement. A single-value lookup would not represent the whole collection. Browser keyboard/touch selection gestures vary, so instructions should not promise one universal modifier key.

Build the two named option groups with Basil and Poppy initially selected. Use name seed for the select, not a different name on each option. The supplied checks inspect markup or local form-data relationships; they do not submit a network request or certify a screen-reader or native-browser experience. Optional local practice: try the changed case in a disposable local page and explain the difference.
after: Add `multiple` to a `<select>` to allow more than one choice. Each selected option sends its own value under the select’s name. The browser does not turn them into one comma-separated answer.

`<optgroup>` puts related options under a group label. The group label is not a choice. Add `selected` to each option you want chosen at the start. `size="4"` asks for four visible rows; it does not limit how many choices can be selected.

This list groups seeds into Herbs and Flowers.

```html
<form id="seeds">
  <label for="choices">Seeds to request</label>
  <select id="choices" name="seed" multiple size="4">
    <optgroup label="Herbs"><option value="basil" selected>Basil</option><option value="dill">Dill</option></optgroup>
    <optgroup label="Flowers"><option value="poppy" selected>Poppy</option></optgroup>
  </select>
  <button type="submit">Request seeds</button>
</form>
```

The select has the name `seed`. Basil and Poppy start selected, so the data contains `seed=basil` and `seed=poppy`. Dill is not selected, so it is left out.

Build form `seeds` with the labeled select `choices`. Use name `seed`, `multiple` and size `4`. Add the Herbs group with Basil and Dill, then the Flowers group with Poppy. Start with Basil and Poppy selected. Run the checks and try changing the choices; selection controls can differ between keyboards and touch screens.
